about: The citizens of the city of Rome (places_rome.gd, citizen.gd): names, the jobs they walk the city at (docs/rome-jobs.md has the full list), and what they say. {name} is their name, {home} the part of the city they live in, {partner} and {kids} their family, {patron} the great house they belong to.

jobs.title: baker
jobs.intro: {name}. The bakery with the mill behind it. I own two donkeys and three slaves, and I owe money on all five.
work: The slaves turn the mill when the donkeys go lame. Chained, some bakeries. Not mine. Mine just can't run far.
The aediles weigh my loaves. Short weight is a fine. Twice short and they close you, and then who feeds my family?
Flour dust gets in your lungs. Old bakers cough blood. I'm not old yet.
worry: When the grain ships are late the crowd blames the bakers. They burned one out on the Aventine in the last shortage.

rise.intro: {name}. Baker. Before the war we ground our own grain at home. Now there's a bakery on every street, and I'm proud of mine.
work: I baked for the legions going south. Hard biscuit, a month's worth to a man. I'd like to think some of it went to Zama.
My word is my measure. A short loaf in this street and you'd never sell another. A Roman's word is worth his weight.
worry: My brother fell at Cannae. I bake for his widow's house as well as mine. That's what brothers are for.

jobs.title: miller
jobs.intro: {name}. I work the mill boats on the river, since the Goths cut the aqueducts.
work: The current turns the wheels. In the siege we ground under arrows. Two of us took one each.
There's grain when the Emperor's ships come and none when they don't. Then the mills stand and people eat grass.
worry: If they cut the river too, we're done for. They'd do it if they could.

jobs.title: butcher
jobs.intro: {name}, butcher. Pork mostly, beef when the market has it.
work: The meat from the sacrifices comes to us to sell. The god gets the smoke, the priest gets the price, I get the flies.
In summer, meat turns by noon. You salt it, you smoke it, or you sell it quick to people who can't be fussy.
Half this street buys from me on credit. I write it on the wall. Some of those names are dead now.
worry: My landlord raised the rent at the Kalends. Where else would I go? He knows it.

rise.intro: {name}, butcher.
work: Meat's for festivals and sacrifices. Most days we eat porridge like our grandfathers, and we're stronger for it.
The best cuts go to the gods first. You don't cheat the gods, and you don't cheat your neighbours.
worry: Prices went mad in the war. We held them down on this street. You don't grow fat on a city at war.

hero.intro: {name}, butcher.
work: Meat for the feasts and the gods. Porridge the rest of the week. We're a porridge people, and proud of it.
The Greeks call us pultiphagi, porridge-eaters. Let them. The porridge-eaters are winning.
worry: Honest weights. The aediles check, but they needn't.

jobs.title: fishmonger
jobs.intro: {name}. Fish. From Ostia when I can get it, from the river when I can't.
work: Don't buy fish caught below the Cloaca. Everything the city throws away comes out there. Everything.
A big mullet sold for more than a slave once. The rich eat what the poor could live on for a year.
Salt fish from Spain keeps. Fresh fish is gone by noon or it's gone off.
worry: They pulled a body out by the island this morning. A woman. Nobody's come asking.

rise.intro: {name}. Fish from the river and the coast.
work: My husband rowed in the fleet against Carthage. He came home. Many didn't. I sell fish; he mends the nets.
The river gives, the gods take their share. We don't complain.
worry: The fleet's been burned at Carthage now. Five hundred ships, they say. The sea's ours.

hero.intro: {name}. Fish.
work: From the river and from Ostia when the salt boats bring it. Rome's no sea city. Not yet.
My husband fought at Sentinum and came home. I sold fish every day he was gone, and prayed every night.
worry: The river gives. The gods give. We give back.

jobs.title: greengrocer
jobs.intro: {name}. I rent a plot outside the gate and walk in before dawn with the donkey.
work: Leeks, cabbages, beans. The rich buy what's new. The poor buy what's left at dusk, cheaper, soft.
The owner of my plot is a senator I've never seen. His steward takes a third.
worry: Robbers on the road at night. Last month they took the donkey and broke my brother's arm.

rise.intro: {name}. I farm a plot outside the Colline Gate, as my father did, and bring the vegetables in at dawn.
work: Cabbage and beans and hard work. Cato says the farmer makes the bravest soldier. He's right. I was one.
Sixteen years I was with the legions. The farm went to weeds. My wife kept it alive. Now I'm home, and it's mine again.
worry: My sons will serve when they're called. As I did. As their grandfather did.

hero.intro: {name}. I farm four iugera outside the gate, like everyone who matters. Curius Dentatus farms seven, and he beat the Samnites.
work: The Samnite envoys found Curius at his hearth boiling turnips, and offered him gold. He said he'd rather rule men who had gold than have it. Then he went back to his turnips.
Plough in spring, march in summer, harvest when you're home. A Roman's year.
worry: They say King Pyrrhus has elephants. Well. We've oxen, and more sense.

jobs.title: fruit seller
jobs.intro: {name}. Fruit, in season. I buy from the growers at the gate and sell it here.
work: Figs from Tusculum, apples from the hills. The margin's thin and the wasps take their share.
My husband sold fruit on this corner. The fever took him three summers ago. I kept the corner.
worry: Summer's the fever season. You sell more fruit and you bury more people.

jobs.title: oil seller
jobs.intro: {name}. Oil, for lamps, cooking, the baths.
work: Good oil from Venafrum, cheap oil from Spain. Some sellers cut it with worse. I don't. Mostly.
A cracked jar in the storeroom and a month's profit runs into the drain.
worry: I borrowed to buy this stock at twelve in the hundred. If prices fall before I sell, I'm finished.

jobs.title: wine seller
jobs.intro: {name}. Wine. Falernian for those with money, the rough red for everyone else.
work: Most of what I sell goes to men drinking away what they earned today, before their wives can get it.
Water it down, the aediles say, and they check my measures. Nobody checks what's in the jars from Campania.
worry: A man died in the street outside last winter. Too drunk to find his door, too cold to wake.

jobs.title: innkeeper
jobs.intro: {name}, and this is my inn. Beds upstairs, stew and wine down here, and don't ask about the back room.
work: Carters, drovers, soldiers on leave, men who don't want to be found. I don't ask names.
The girls upstairs pay me for the rooms. It's legal. They're registered with the aediles. Most of them.
Dice in the back. Illegal, except at the Saturnalia. The aediles' men drink here free, so.
worry: A lodger cut another's throat over a debt in the spring. The blood's still in the floorboards.

rise.intro: {name}. An inn by the gate, for travellers and carters.
work: Soldiers coming home stop here first. Some weep to see the city. Some weep because their fathers aren't in it.
An honest measure and a clean bed. The aediles look in, and they find nothing to say.
worry: Too many veterans with nowhere to go yet. The Senate's promised land. It'll come.

hero.intro: {name}. An inn by the Capene Gate. Soldiers, drovers, Sabines coming to market.
work: The Sabines were our enemies in my grandfather's day. Now they're Romans, near enough, and drink my wine and complain about it. Family, you see.
The Samnites? Tough men, good fighters, terrible singers. We've fought them for fifty years and made peace at last.
worry: No trouble in my inn. One look from my wife and the fiercest Umbrian goes quiet.

jobs.title: cook-shop keeper
jobs.intro: {name}. Hot food at my counter. Chickpeas, lentils, a bit of sausage.
work: No one in the flats can cook. No kitchen, and the landlords forbid fires. So they eat here or not at all.
The Senate keeps trying to ban hot food in cook-shops. They say it's where the poor plot. The poor are too tired to plot.
worry: A fire starts in one of these places every month somewhere in Rome. Mine won't be the one.

jobs.title: sausage seller
jobs.intro: {name}. Sausages, from the tray. The baths, the games, wherever the crowds are.
work: I buy from the butcher at dawn and have to sell it all by dark. What's left, my family eats. Every night.
worry: My daughter's sick. The Greek doctor wants more than I make in a month.

jobs.title: pastry cook
jobs.intro: {name}. Cakes: honey cakes, cheese cakes, sacrificial cakes for the temples.
work: The temples buy the most. People who can't afford a lamb offer a cake shaped like one.
Libum for a birthday: cheese, flour, an egg, baked on bay leaves. For the man's genius, his guardian spirit.
worry: Honey's dear this year. I pay it or I lose the temple trade.

jobs.title: water carrier
jobs.intro: {name}. I carry water up to the high floors for the families who pay my master.
work: Rich houses have a pipe from the aqueduct. The fifth floor has me. Forty trips a day.
My master rents me out by the day. I see a copper of it at the Saturnalia.
worry: The last water carrier here fell on the stairs with two jars. He didn't get up. They bought me the next week.

rise.intro: {name}. I carry water from the Appian aqueduct fountains up to the houses.
work: Censor Appius brought the water in a hundred years ago. Rome builds for its grandchildren.
My master is a fair man. He fought at Cannae and lived. He says a household is a small Republic.
worry: I hope to earn my freedom. Serve well, and the master keeps his word. That's Roman fides.

jobs.title: fuller
jobs.intro: {name}, fuller. Wool cleaned and whitened.
work: We tread the cloth in vats of urine and fuller's earth. I pay for the urine: pots on the corners, collected every morning.
Then sulphur smoke to bleach it. It rots your chest. Fullers die young and smell of it the whole way.
The law says if I ruin a toga I pay for it. A senator's toga costs more than my slave.
worry: The vapours. Two of my men cough all night. One's coughing blood now.

rise.intro: {name}, fuller.
work: White togas for the Campus: when a man stands for office he wears the whitened toga, the candida. We make him candidatus.
Honest work, hard work. The smell is the price of clean wool.
worry: Our guild honours Minerva at her festival. We'll pour for her this spring.

hero.intro: {name}, fuller.
work: The candidates want their togas white as snow for the Campus. Candidatus: that's where the word comes from, from us.
It's a smelly trade and an honest one. Nobody ever lied about a clean toga.
worry: My guild keeps Minerva's feast. We sing badly and drink well.

jobs.title: cobbler
jobs.intro: {name}, cobbler.
work: Soldiers' boots, ladies' slippers, senators' red shoes. I make them; I've never worn anything but these.
I was a slave in a big house, making the family's shoes. They freed me when I was forty. I kept the trade and lost the roof.
worry: Leather's gone up. The tanners across the river set the price together and dare anyone to argue.

rise.intro: {name}, cobbler.
work: Soldiers' boots, mostly: hobnailed, to march a hundred miles. The legions walked to Africa on boots from shops like mine.
Honest leather, honest stitching. A boot that splits on the march can kill a man.
worry: My son's in the levy this year. I made his boots myself.

hero.intro: {name}, cobbler.
work: The Appian Way goes all the way to Capua now. Blind old Appius built it, and the army walks it in my boots.
A good boot and a good conscience: you can walk a long way on both.
worry: Leather's cheap and the customers are honest. What more could a cobbler want?

jobs.title: clothes dealer
jobs.intro: {name}. Tunics, cloaks, second-hand togas.
work: Half my stock is dead men's clothes. The heirs sell the lot. It's all still good wool.
Thieves at the baths steal cloaks and try to sell them to me. I know the good ones by sight. I send them away. Usually.
worry: The fire last year took my whole shop. I'm still paying for the stock that burned.

jobs.title: weaver
jobs.intro: {name}. I weave.
work: Paid by the piece, by a dealer who sets the price. When my eyes go, so does the living.
The tombstones praise a woman who worked wool and kept the house. Nobody puts the price of the wool on them.
worry: My husband drinks what I make. He's the man of the house, the law says. The law's never been to our house.

rise.intro: {name}. I weave, as my mother did.
work: A Roman woman works wool and keeps her house: that's the praise on the old tombs, and it's a good praise.
In the war the women gave their gold to the treasury, and wove for the legions. We'd do it again.
worry: Four sons. Two are with the legions. I weave their cloaks myself.

hero.intro: {name}. I weave, like Lucretia did, at her loom in the night when the other wives were feasting.
work: The old women tell us about the Sabine wives who ran between the armies, their babies in their arms, and made the two peoples one. My grandmother was a Sabine.
A good woman keeps the hearth and the wool. And her tongue, if she's wise. I'm not always wise.
worry: My husband's with the army in the south. I've woven him two cloaks. He'll lose one, men always do.

jobs.title: purple dealer
jobs.intro: {name}, from Tyre. Purple, the real thing, from the shellfish.
work: The dye works at home stink for miles. The men who crush the shells don't live long. The senators who wear it do.
Ten thousand shells for a little dye. That's what a stripe on a tunic means: somebody else's work, and a lot of it.
worry: The laws against luxury come and go. When they come, nobody buys, and I still owe the shippers.

jobs.title: blacksmith
jobs.intro: {name}. Smith.
work: Hinges, nails, knives. And shackles. The slave dealers pay well and pay on time.
Burns on every finger. My father lost an eye to a spark. You learn to turn your face away.
worry: The neighbours complain about the noise. The landlord says one more complaint and I'm out.

rise.intro: {name}. Smith.
work: Through the war I made nothing but swords and spear points, day and night. The Senate paid late and I didn't mind.
A sword I made went to Zama in a young man's hand. He came to tell me it held. I've never been prouder.
worry: Iron's scarce. Everything went to the legions. We'll rebuild.

hero.intro: {name}. Smith. Ploughshares in spring, spear points in summer.
work: The Samnites taught us the javelin and the long shield. We took the best of them and beat them with it. That's the Roman way.
My hammer rings from dawn. Rome's growing, and everything it grows needs iron.
worry: Some say the Greeks make finer blades. Then why do they hire Romans to fight?

jobs.title: goldsmith
jobs.intro: {name}. Goldsmith, on the Sacred Way.
work: I was my master's slave and learned the trade in his shop. When he freed me I took his name and, quietly, some of his customers.
Rings, brooches, gold leaf for the statues. A woman came in yesterday to sell her mother's jewellery to pay a debt. I paid her a third of what it's worth. So would anyone.
worry: Gold walks. I keep a dog and a slave who sleeps across the door.

jobs.title: potter
jobs.intro: {name}. Pots.
work: The kiln's outside the wall, for the fires. The clay's from the river. The children dig it.
Every pot that cracks in the kiln is a meal someone in my house doesn't eat.
worry: My oldest boy wants to be a soldier. Twenty-five years. At least they feed you.

rise.intro: {name}. Potter.
work: Plain pots for plain people. The rich want painted Greek ware. My grandmother would have smashed it.
The clay's from the river, the kiln's outside the wall, and the work is honest.
worry: Two apprentices went to the war. One came back. I'll teach his son the wheel.

hero.intro: {name}. I make pots, and good ones, if I say so.
work: The Greeks of Tarentum paint theirs all over with gods and heroes. Ours hold water. I know which I'd rather drink from.
A pot is like a Roman: plain on the outside, sound all through, and hard to break.
worry: My boy wants to be a soldier like his uncles. He can throw a spear before he can write his name.

jobs.title: lamp maker
jobs.intro: {name}. Oil lamps.
work: Gladiators on the top sell best. Men dying, for people to read by. Nobody thinks about it.
Lovers sell too, for the brothels and the newly married. I make both from the same clay.
worry: A lamp knocked over in a top-floor room: that's how most fires start. Nobody blames the lamp maker. Yet.

jobs.title: perfumer
jobs.intro: {name}. Perfumes, oils, ointments.
work: Rose from Campania, nard from India. Weight for weight, more than silver.
The ladies buy it, the men buy more, and the undertakers buy the most. For the dead, and for the smell of them.
worry: The old senators want it banned as effeminate. Their wives are my best customers.

jobs.title: bookseller
jobs.intro: {name}. Books. Copied by my own slaves.
work: Twenty copies of a new poem by the Nones. The poet gets nothing but his name. I get the money.
Some books you don't sell openly. Pamphlets against powerful men. Someone always wants them. Someone always finds out.
worry: A bookseller was flogged last year for copying a book the Senate had burned. I sold three copies of it myself.

jobs.title: money changer
jobs.intro: {name}. I change money and test coin.
work: A bad coin rings flat. Silver-plated copper. The forgers get crucified. The mint cheapens the silver and nobody gets anything.
People come to me when they're desperate: a ring to sell, a debt due by sunset. I give them a fair price. Fair for me.
worry: When a debtor runs, I'm the one out of pocket.

jobs.title: moneylender
jobs.intro: {name}. I lend money. Twelve in the hundred, a year. That's the legal rate.
work: The legal rate. For those I trust. For the rest, there are other arrangements.
A man who can't pay sells his slaves, then his furniture, then his daughter's dowry. Then I take the lease.
The senators lend too, through freedmen like me, so their hands stay clean. Brutus lent to a whole city at forty-eight.
worry: People spit when I pass. They still come at night to borrow.

jobs.title: slave dealer
jobs.intro: {name}. I deal in slaves. Mostly from the East, some from the wars.
work: They stand on the platform by the Temple of Castor with chalk on their feet and a placard round their necks: origin, age, skills, faults.
The law says I must declare if one's sick, or a runaway, or has tried to kill himself. So I declare it, quietly.
Everyone despises my trade. Everyone buys.
worry: One hanged himself on the ship last month. A loss. The buyers don't want to hear about it.

jobs.title: prostitute
jobs.intro: {name}. You know what I am. I'm on the aediles' register, if you're asking.
work: The keeper of the house takes most of it. What's left pays for the room I sleep in.
Some of the girls were sold into it as children. I came to it because the other choice was starving.
The law says we can't wear the stola like a respectable woman. We wear the toga, like men. They mean it as shame.
worry: When I'm older I'll be put out. Nobody wants an old woman in a doorway in the Subura.
call: Come in out of the cold.

jobs.title: barber
jobs.intro: {name}, barber.
work: A barber hears everything: who's in debt, who's sleeping with whom, who's been denounced. I keep most of it to myself.
Razor, water, no soap. If I cut you, a cobweb soaked in vinegar stops the bleeding.
worry: A barber on the next street cut a man's throat. An accident, he said. The man's brother said otherwise.

rise.intro: {name}, barber. Barbers came to Rome from Sicily in my grandfather's day. Before that the Romans wore their beards like the old kings.
work: The young nobles want clean chins now, the Greek way. Their grandfathers wore beards and conquered Italy.
I hear the talk in this chair: the war, the Senate, the price of grain. And I keep it here.
worry: My brother is with the army still, in Africa, till the treaty's signed.

hero.intro: {name}. One of the first barbers in Rome. My father came from Sicily with the trade.
work: Before us, Romans wore their beards and hair long, like the old kings on the statues. Now the young men want their chins bare. My fortune!
The old men still won't shave. They say a beard is honest. I say it's a place for soup.
worry: Everyone talks in the chair: the Samnites, Pyrrhus, the harvest. Mostly the harvest.

jobs.title: doctor
jobs.intro: {name}, a doctor, trained at Pergamon.
work: Half the children in the flats die before they're five. I can't stop fevers. I can bleed people and pray.
The rich call me to their villas. The poor go to the temple of Aesculapius on the island and sleep there, hoping for a dream.
Owners leave sick slaves on the island to die rather than pay a doctor. I've treated a few there for nothing. Most still die.
worry: If a patient dies it's my fault. If he lives, the gods did it.

rise.intro: {name}, a doctor, from Greece. There are few of us in Rome yet.
work: Romans trust cabbage and their grandfathers' remedies. Old men here call my art a Greek trick.
The wounded from the war taught me more than any book at home. The Romans don't complain under the knife.
worry: They are a hard people and a straight people. A man's word here is his bond. It's not like that everywhere.

jobs.title: midwife
jobs.intro: {name}. Midwife.
work: The birthing stool, warm oil, clean linen, a steady voice. Then it's the gods and the mother's strength.
Not every mother lives. I've closed the eyes of women younger than my daughter.
Sometimes the father says the child's not to be raised. It goes to the Columna Lactaria, or the dung heap, and someone may take it. Usually a dealer.
worry: The ones you lose stay with you. I count them at night.

rise.intro: {name}. Midwife.
work: Children are the city's strength. After Cannae every house wanted sons. I've brought hundreds.
Not every mother lives, and not every child. We bury them with honour and go on.
worry: The census counts citizens by their children. Rome counts its future in cradles.

jobs.title: schoolmaster
jobs.intro: {name}. I teach letters and sums, under the awning, dawn till noon.
work: The boys chant, the neighbours shout at us, I shout at the boys. The cane does the rest. Their fathers insist.
Only the ones whose parents can pay. The girls, if they're lucky, learn at home. The slaves' children learn nothing.
worry: Half the fathers don't pay on time. Some never.

rise.intro: {name}. I teach letters and sums, and the Twelve Tables by heart, as every boy must.
work: The boys chant the laws of the Twelve Tables: 'If a man is summoned to court, he shall go.' It's in their bones by ten.
Their fathers teach them to ride, swim, throw a spear and fear the gods. I teach them to read what the laws say.
worry: Half my older boys are in the levy. I pray for them by name.

jobs.title: boy's tutor
jobs.intro: {name}. I take the young master to school and see he gets there, and back.
work: A Greek slave for a Roman boy: it teaches him Greek and teaches him who's master.
If he misbehaves, I'm the one beaten. That's the arrangement.
worry: They say I'll be freed when he comes of age. They said that to the last one.

jobs.title: crier
jobs.intro: {name}! Crier and auctioneer.
work: Auctions of the goods of debtors and the dead. I shout the price, somebody's whole life goes for a fraction.
Runaway slaves: name, description, reward. Most are brought back. What happens then isn't my business.
worry: You lose your voice, you lose your living.
call: Hear ye! Auction at noon by the Temple of Castor!
Runaway! A Syrian, answers to Eros, reward for his return!

rise.intro: {name}! Crier!
work: The levy is called on the Capitol at dawn. Every man of military age, by tribe. Rome needs her sons.
The Senate's decrees, the games, the festivals: I cry them all.
worry: I cried the news of Cannae in this Forum. I cried the news of Zama. I'll never forget either.

hero.intro: {name}! Crier!
work: Hear ye: the Senate has refused the peace of King Pyrrhus! Old Appius Claudius, blind as he is, had himself carried in and said Rome makes no peace with a king in Italy!
Hear ye: Fabricius the consul went to Pyrrhus's camp, and the king offered him gold, and he laughed, and the king set an elephant roaring behind him, and he didn't even turn round!
worry: Some days I have nothing to cry but the price of beans. Those days I cry it proudly.

jobs.title: carpenter
jobs.intro: {name}. Carpenter. Floors, roofs, the frames for the concrete.
work: They build them six storeys on footings meant for three. I build what I'm paid for and I don't sleep on the top floor.
Our guild has a burial fund. Nine of us were killed last year when a block came down while we were raising it.
worry: When a block collapses, the owner blames the builder, the builder blames the owner, and the dead are dead.

rise.intro: {name}. Carpenter.
work: We rebuilt the temples the lightning hit, and the houses the floods took. There's always building in a growing city.
Our guild's older than the Republic. King Numa founded the guilds, they say.
worry: Timber comes from the Sabine hills. The ships took most of it in the war.

hero.intro: {name}. Carpenter. Houses, barns, the bridge.
work: The Sublician bridge has no iron in it at all, not a nail. The gods of the river wouldn't like it. Horatius held it once against a whole army while they cut it down behind him.
Then he swam the Tiber in his armour. Or so my father told it. Every father tells it a little better.
worry: Timber, pegs, and a straight eye. The city's growing faster than we can build it.

jobs.title: marble mason
jobs.intro: {name}. Marble.
work: White from Luna, yellow from Numidia, purple from Egypt. Quarried by convicts who die in the dust.
Epitaphs mostly. 'Aged four years, five months, three days.' I cut a lot of those. Too many.
worry: The dust settles in your chest. Old masons cough themselves to death.

jobs.title: wall painter
jobs.intro: {name}. I paint walls: red panels, black, gardens with birds for those who'll never see a real one.
work: You paint while the plaster's wet so it lasts. The owner watches in case we steal the cinnabar.
Cinnabar is mined by condemned men in Spain. The mercury in it kills them. It makes a lovely red.
worry: Some owners don't pay the last third. What am I going to do, take them to court?

jobs.title: plasterer
jobs.intro: {name}. Plasterer.
work: Three coats of lime and sand, three of marble dust, done properly. The landlords want one coat and paint.
The lime eats your hands to the bone if you're careless. I've seen it.
worry: Work dries up in winter. So does food.

jobs.title: porter
jobs.intro: {name}. I carry things.
work: A sack of flour, a jar of oil, a bed up four flights. No carts in the city by day, so it all goes on men's backs.
My owner hires me out. My back will be finished before I'm forty. Then he'll sell me cheap, or free me so he needn't feed me.
worry: When my father's back went, they left him on the island of Aesculapius. We never heard if he lived.

rise.intro: {name}. I carry loads.
work: My back is strong and the city's growing. There's work for anyone who'll do it.
The master rents me out, and he gives me a share. I'm saving for my freedom.
worry: Rome was built on backs like mine. I don't mind. I'd like it built on my son's too, as a free man.

jobs.title: sack carrier
jobs.intro: {name}. I unload the grain barges at the port.
work: Sixty pounds a sack, barge to warehouse. The clerk marks a tally for each. He always marks one short.
The city eats that much grain because it has to be fed or it riots. We're the ones who carry the peace on our backs.
worry: A man fell between the barge and the quay last week. They pulled the barge off him too late.

rise.intro: {name}. I carry the grain from the barges.
work: Sicily's grain feeds us now, and Sardinia's. The war paid for itself in the end.
Hard work, and honest. The tally-man counts true. His father did too.
worry: I carried grain the day the news of Zama came. We dropped the sacks and cheered till we were hoarse.

jobs.title: muleteer
jobs.intro: {name}. Muleteer. I bring the carts in at night.
work: Carts are banned by day, so the whole city's food comes in after dark. Rome eats well and sleeps badly.
Robbers wait on the roads outside the gates. I carry a club. I've used it.
worry: The mule's worth more than I am, on paper.

rise.intro: {name}. Muleteer.
work: I drove supply carts for the legions in Italy while Hannibal was loose in it. The roads the censors built won that war as much as the swords.
A good road, a good mule, an honest load. Rome runs on all three.
worry: The country's still half empty from the war. The farms need men.

jobs.title: litter bearer
jobs.intro: {name}. I carry my master's litter. Eight of us, matched for height.
work: He reads inside. We sweat. We hear everything he says to his friends. Nobody thinks we have ears.
If one stumbles, all of us are whipped.
worry: The Clivus Capitolinus, uphill, in August, with a fat man inside.

jobs.title: boatman
jobs.intro: {name}. I run a boat on the Tiber.
work: Oxen haul us upstream from Ostia on the towpath. The haulers are slaves or men in debt. Same thing, most days.
The river gives back what people throw in. Rubbish, dogs, sometimes a baby. You learn not to look.
worry: Floods in spring. The river comes into the Forum and the low flats, and people drown in their beds.

rise.intro: {name}. Boatman on the Tiber.
work: I rowed the grain up from Ostia through the whole war, even when Hannibal was at the gates. Rome never starved.
My son's at sea with the fleet. The Romans learned the sea from the Carthaginians and beat them on it.
worry: The river's ours now, and the sea.

hero.intro: {name}. Boatman.
work: Up the river with salt, down the river with grain. Old Ostia's small still, but the river's generous.
We don't much trust the sea. The Tarentines do, and look where it got them.
worry: The Tiber took my grandfather. My father pulled him out. Both got better.

jobs.title: bath keeper
jobs.intro: {name}. I run the baths down the street.
work: The furnace slaves work under the floors in the heat all day. They don't live long. I buy more.
Women in the morning, men in the afternoon. Some baths mix them. Those have a reputation.
worry: Thieves steal clothes from the benches. I'm blamed for it by the customer and fined for it by the aediles.

jobs.title: diviner
jobs.intro: {name}, haruspex, from Etruria. I read the liver of the victim.
work: Senators hire me before a vote, generals before a battle. They pay for the answer they wanted.
Every part of the liver belongs to a god. A bad liver has stopped wars. A convenient one has started them.
worry: Some young men laugh at the old arts. Most of them ask me in private when someone's ill.

rise.intro: {name}, haruspex, from Etruria. The Senate calls us when the signs are strange.
work: In the war the prodigies came thick: showers of stones, a talking ox, blood in the streams. The Senate expiated every one. Nothing was neglected.
Rome is the most pious city I know. They fear the gods, and it's made them masters of the world.
worry: Men speak of the Greek philosophers who doubt the gods. Let them doubt somewhere else.

hero.intro: {name}, from Etruria. We taught the Romans to read the signs, when they were still farmers on seven hills.
work: They are a strange people. They take the gods more seriously than the gods do.
When the signs are bad they stop everything: the vote, the battle, the march. And then they win anyway.
worry: My grandfather said Rome would be great. The liver said it. The Romans said: we know.

jobs.title: temple keeper
jobs.intro: {name}. I keep this temple.
work: People leave clay limbs when a limb's healed, and lead tablets when they want someone harmed. I'm meant to take those down. I read them first.
A curse tablet this morning: a woman wanted her husband's lover's tongue to rot. She nailed it through, to be sure.
worry: The temple treasury is where men deposit money for safe keeping. Where there's money there are thieves.

rise.intro: {name}. I keep this temple.
work: People bring thanks for sons home from the war. More this year than in all the war together.
The temple treasury holds the city's money and the people's vows. Nobody has ever stolen from it. It's unthinkable.
worry: Rome keeps faith with the gods and the gods keep faith with Rome. That's why we won.

jobs.title: sacrificial attendant
jobs.intro: {name}. I lead the beasts to the altar and do the killing.
work: A beast that goes quietly is a good omen, so you calm it. Then the hammer, then the knife.
If it bolts, the rite is spoiled, and the whole thing starts again with another beast. The magistrate is not pleased.
worry: Some days I kill thirty. The smell never leaves your hair.

rise.intro: {name}. I serve at the altar.
work: The ox goes willing if the rite is done rightly. The gods watch how we do things, not just what.
In the war we did everything to win the gods back after Cannae: the Sibylline books, the Great Mother brought from Phrygia. And they came back to us.
worry: The victory was the gods' before it was Scipio's. We must not forget it.

hero.intro: {name}. I lead the beast to the altar.
work: The rite must be done exactly, word for word. A single word wrong and the priest begins again.
The gods are near here. You can feel them on the Capitol, in the groves, at the springs. They like us, I think. We keep faith.
worry: Our gods are plain gods, like us. The Greeks' gods squabble like a bad family.

jobs.title: undertaker
jobs.intro: {name}. Undertaker.
work: The rich get pipers, mourners, a pyre on the Appian Way. The poor get a burial club if they paid in, or the pits on the Esquiline if they didn't.
In a fever summer we can't dig fast enough. We burn them in lots.
worry: Undertakers live outside decent company. We're polluted by the work. People need us and won't eat with us.

rise.intro: {name}. Undertaker.
work: A great man's funeral: his ancestors walk before him, men wearing the wax masks of every consul in the family. His son praises him from the Rostra. The young men watch and burn to be worthy.
We buried so many in the war there were no masks left to carry. The Senate limited mourning to thirty days. There was a war to win.
worry: Death for Rome is the best death. The whole city says so, and means it.

jobs.title: corpse bearer
jobs.intro: {name}. I carry the bodies out, at night, the ones nobody pays for.
work: Out through the Esquiline gate to the pits. The smell of them reaches the city when the wind turns.
Babies, mostly, and old slaves, and the ones found in the street in the morning.
worry: Nobody looks at me. That's how they like it.

jobs.title: piper
jobs.intro: {name}. Piper.
work: At a sacrifice the pipe drowns any unlucky word. At a funeral it covers the crying.
Funerals pay steadiest. The law limits us to ten pipers at a funeral. The rich break it.
worry: I play at the brothels too, some nights. Music's music.

rise.intro: {name}. Piper.
work: At the sacrifice my pipe covers any ill-omened word. The rite must be perfect.
At the funerals of the war dead I played till my lips bled.
worry: Music for the gods and for the dead. That's a piper's life, and it's a good one.

hero.intro: {name}. Piper.
work: Weddings, sacrifices, funerals, harvests. I play and the city dances, or weeps, or eats.
The pipers once walked out to Tibur in a sulk. The Senate got them drunk and carted them home asleep. We still celebrate it every June, in masks.
worry: The Greeks have finer music. We have better reasons to play.

jobs.title: street performer
jobs.intro: {name}. Actor, mime, whatever pays.
work: Actors are infames: disgraced by law. We can't vote in the same way, can't give evidence. We can make the Senate laugh.
The mimes play adulteries and stupid husbands. The crowd roars. Half of them are the husbands.
worry: Mock the wrong man and you're flogged. It's happened to better men than me.

jobs.title: charioteer
jobs.intro: {name}. I drive for the Greens.
work: Four horses, seven laps, the turn close enough to scrape the post. A crash there kills men and horses both.
Win enough and you're freed, and rich. Most of us die before twenty-five.
worry: The Blues put curse tablets under the starting gates. They name my horses and ask the gods to break their legs.

jobs.title: gladiator
jobs.intro: {name}. Thracian style. Eleven fights.
work: The loser lives if the crowd and the giver of the games want him to. Most do. Some days they don't.
We swear the oath at the school: to be burned, bound, beaten, killed by the sword. I said it aloud with forty others.
worry: I've killed two men I ate beside. The school doesn't let you choose.

jobs.title: gladiator trainer
jobs.intro: {name}. I own a troupe of gladiators.
work: I hire them out to whoever gives games. If one dies, I'm paid for him, fifty times what he cost to feed.
People despise my trade the way they despise pimps. They pay for seats all the same.
worry: Dead gladiators are expensive. Living ones are expensive. It's a hard business.

jobs.title: clerk
jobs.intro: {name}. Clerk of the treasury, under the Temple of Saturn.
work: Magistrates come and go every year. We stay. We know which accounts not to look at too closely.
A new quaestor wanted to audit everything. His patron had a word. He stopped.
worry: If the accounts are ever properly checked, somebody will need to be blamed. It's usually the clerk.

jobs.title: lictor
jobs.intro: {name}. Lictor. I carry the rods before the magistrate.
work: The rods are for beating. The axe is for killing. Inside the city the axe stays out, because a citizen can appeal.
A slave can't appeal. A foreigner often can't. The rods don't ask.
worry: I've flogged men in the Forum on a magistrate's word. You don't let yourself think about it.

rise.intro: {name}. Lictor to the consul.
work: The rods and the axe: the power of the Roman people, carried before its magistrate. Inside the city the axe comes out: a citizen may appeal.
The consul's power is great and lasts a year, and then he goes back to his farm. That's the Republic.
worry: I walked before the consul who marched to Africa. I've never seen men so glad to serve.

hero.intro: {name}. Lictor.
work: The rods and the axe. I carry them before the consul. He carries the Republic.

Mucius, the young man who sneaked into the Etruscan king's camp to kill him? Caught, he held his right hand in the fire until it burned, to show what Romans are. The king let him go. They called him Scaevola, left-hand. Every lictor knows that story.
worry: The consul goes back to his plough when his year is done. So do I, to mine.

jobs.title: watchman
jobs.intro: {name}. Of the vigiles. Fire and theft.
work: Buckets, axes, hooks to pull a burning wall down, blankets soaked in vinegar. Some nights none of it's enough.
Most of us are freedmen. Six years' service, and the state makes you a citizen. If you live that long.
worry: Last month we pulled eleven bodies from an insula in the Subura. Four were children. The owner was at his villa.

jobs.title: soldier
jobs.intro: {name}. Soldier. I keep order.
work: We break up riots at the games and the grain lines. When ordered, we break heads.
Pay's on time in the city. On the frontier you might wait a year and eat bark.
worry: Some nights it's knives in the alleys. Some nights it's a whole quarter burning.

jobs.title: veteran
jobs.intro: {name}. Twenty years under the eagles. I've got the scars and not much else.
work: They promised land when we were discharged. I got a plot on bad soil in Samnium and sold it to pay debts.
I left the fingers of my left hand in Gaul. The man next to me left his head.
worry: I sleep badly. So does everyone who was there.

rise.intro: {name}. I served under Scipio. Spain, then Africa. I was at Zama.
work: Hannibal's elephants came at us and we opened the lines and let them through, like he told us. Then we closed and held. We held.
Many of us were Cannae men: disgraced, sent to Sicily, never allowed home. Scipio took us to Africa and we made it right.
worry: Land in Apulia, they say. I'll farm it and send my sons when Rome calls.

hero.intro: {name}. I was at Sentinum. The day of the Gauls and the Samnites together, and Decius.
work: I saw him ride out. He'd spoken the words with the priest, head veiled, standing on a spear. Then he rode into the Gauls and the gods took him and the line held.
The Caudine Forks, my father remembered: an army sent under the yoke by the Samnites, bent double under the spears. We paid it back. Rome always pays it back.
worry: The Greeks with their elephants and their phalanx. Let them come to the Campus and see.

jobs.title: senator
jobs.intro: I am {name}. My family has sat in the Senate for generations.
work: Elections are bought. Everyone knows. The question is only who buys more, and who's caught.
Trade is beneath a senator. So I own the land, and the freedmen who trade, and the ships they trade in.
My clients vote as I tell them. In return they eat. That's how the Republic works, whatever the philosophers say.
worry: My son borrowed ruinously to buy an aedileship and the games that go with it. If he loses the next election, we lose the house.

rise.intro: I am {name}. My family has given Rome consuls and soldiers since the kings.
work: Three of my brothers fell at Cannae. The Senate did not ask for peace. Not one senator spoke of peace. That is Rome.
We refused to ransom the prisoners Hannibal took. A soldier who surrenders is lost to Rome. It was cruel. It was right.
worry: Luxury is creeping in from the Greek cities. Silver plate, perfumes, dancing. It softens men. We must hold the line.

hero.intro: I am {name}. I have a farm, a house, a vote in the Senate, and three sons in the legions. A rich man, by our reckoning.
work: Decius Mus, at Sentinum, fifteen years ago: the Gauls were breaking our line, so he vowed himself and the enemy to the gods below, and rode into them alone. His father had done the same against the Latins. We won both days.
The Tarentines laughed at our envoy's Greek and dirtied his toga. He told them it would be washed in their blood. Now Pyrrhus is here with his elephants. Let him come.
worry: We have no silver plate and want none. Curius had one earthenware cup. Fabricius, as censor, threw a man out of the Senate for owning ten pounds of silver plate. That's the Senate I sit in.

jobs.title: client
jobs.intro: {name}. A client of the house of {patron}.
work: At dawn I put on my toga and stand in his hall with a hundred others to greet him. He may not look at me.
The basket of food he gives feeds my family. My vote belongs to him. So does my silence.
worry: If he falls from favour, so do we all. Nobody feeds the clients of a condemned man.

rise.intro: {name}. Client of the house of {patron}.
work: At dawn I greet my patron. When I was in need he helped me, and in the war I fought in his company. Patron and client: it's a bond of faith.
My vote goes with his, because his cause is mine. He'd lose his honour if he failed me.
worry: My father was his father's client. My son will be his son's. That's how Rome holds together.

hero.intro: {name}. Client of the house of {patron}.
work: My patron stood by me in court and I stand by him in battle. Faith for faith. That's the oldest law in Rome, older than the Tables.
He eats turnips, I eat turnips. We're the same Romans, he just has more land to grow them on.
worry: His son and mine are learning the spear together on the Campus.

jobs.title: householder
jobs.intro: I'm {name}.
work: I married at fourteen, to a man my father chose. He's not unkind. That counts for a great deal.
I've buried two of my five children. Every mother I know has buried some.
I run the house: the slaves, the stores, the accounts. In law I can't sign a contract without a guardian.
worry: My husband's been seen with a freedwoman. If he divorces me, the dowry comes back to my father. Not to me.

rise.intro: I'm {name}.
work: When the gold was needed for the war, we women gave our jewels to the treasury. The law since then keeps our dress plain. We keep it proudly.
I run the house and raise the sons. Two are with the legions. I raised them to go.
worry: I buried my husband's brother after Cannae, without a body. Half the city did. We grieved thirty days, as the Senate ordered, and then we went on.

hero.intro: I'm {name}.
work: Veturia, Coriolanus's mother, turned back a whole army by scolding her son. Roman mothers are not to be trifled with.
My sons are with the legions. I sent them off with bread, a blessing, and a clip on the ear to come home proud.
worry: Wool, the hearth, the children, the household gods. And the neighbours' business, if I'm honest.

jobs.title: maid
jobs.intro: {name}. I'm a maid in the house of {patron}. Out for the shopping.
work: The mistress is hard but fair. The master is the one to keep away from, if you can.
My son belongs to the household. They could sell him tomorrow and I'd have no say. I try not to think about it.
worry: I'm saving my allowance to buy my freedom. Twelve years, maybe. By then they'll have raised my price.

rise.intro: {name}. I serve in the house of {patron}.
work: The household works together: the master, the mistress, the children, the slaves. We eat the same bread.
I was born in the house. The master has promised me freedom when his daughter marries. He keeps his word.
worry: The young master is with the army. The whole house prays for him at the hearth.

jobs.title: slave
jobs.intro: {name}. I belong to the house of {patron}.
work: Errands for the steward. Letters, messages, the bread. I know every shortcut in the city.
When the steward's in a temper, it's the nearest back that pays. Mine is usually nearest.
worry: They say I'll be freed before thirty. I'm twenty-nine.

rise.intro: {name}. I belong to the house of {patron}.
work: The master worked the fields beside us before the war. He's a hard man, but he's hard on himself first.
In the worst of the war they armed eight thousand slaves and freed them for their courage. It's remembered.
worry: Serve well, and you'll be freed, and your children will be citizens. That's the Roman way.

hero.intro: {name}. I belong to the house of {patron}. There are only four of us.
work: I eat at the master's table, from the same pot. We plough the same field. He shouts at the ox more than at me.
At the Saturnalia he serves us. He's a terrible cook.
worry: He says he'll free me when his son comes home from the war. I believe him. He's never broken his word to anyone.

jobs.title: merchant
jobs.intro: {name}. A merchant: glass and cloth from Syria, wine going back.
work: Rome makes nothing and buys everything. Its money comes from the provinces, taxes and plunder. I'm just taking a little of it home.
Every harbour has a customs man with his hand out and a Roman who can have you flogged if you complain.
worry: I lost a ship off Sicily last year. Eleven men. I still pay their widows.

rise.intro: {name}, a trader from Massilia. Rome's ally.
work: Romans keep their word. Carthage never did. That's why the cities of the coast chose Rome.
They're a poor city still, hard and plain. They buy little and pay honestly.
worry: Their fides is famous. A treaty with Rome is worth more than a Punic oath.

hero.intro: {name}, trading salt and cloth from Campania.
work: Romans pay what they promise and ask what's fair. It's slow business. It's good business.
Tarentum's rich and proud and hired a king to fight for it. Rome's poor and proud and fights for itself.
worry: The Appian Way's cut my journey in half. Blind Appius knew what he was doing.

jobs.title: priest
jobs.intro: {name}, a priest of the church of this quarter.
work: My grandfather hid in the catacombs when they burned the Scriptures. Now the Emperor builds us basilicas. I don't know which frightens me more.
The sick, the widows, the ones in debt: they come to us because nobody else will have them.
worry: Men buy church offices now like they used to buy magistracies. The same families, the same money.

jobs.title: deacon
jobs.intro: {name}, deacon. I see to the food for the poor.
work: The lists are long, name by name. Widows, orphans, the sick, the old.
When the grain doesn't come, I have to choose who eats. I pray for the ones I don't choose.
worry: People who'd have starved in the old city now come to the Church to eat. They stay for the bread, some for God.

jobs.title: monk
jobs.intro: {name}. A monk.
work: We pray at the hours, work, eat once a day. We nurse the sick when the plague comes. Most of them die anyway.
I was a senator's son. After the siege I gave away what the Goths had left. It wasn't much.
worry: The world is ending, some of the brothers say. Look around. It's hard to argue.

jobs.title: catacomb digger
jobs.intro: {name}. I dig the galleries outside the walls where the Christians bury their dead.
work: Down in the tufa with a lamp and a pick, shelf after shelf, gallery below gallery. Children's graves are the small ones. There are many.
We sell the grave places. Near a martyr costs more. Even the dead pay rent.
worry: The Goths went through the cemeteries looking for gold. There's no gold. Only bones.

jobs.title: beggar
jobs.intro: {name}. A beggar. Spare something?
work: I was a baker once, when there were people to buy bread. Then the siege. Then nothing.
The church steps are best. The Christians are told to give. Some do.
worry: Winter. Two men I slept beside died last winter, one on each side of me.

jobs.title: pilgrim
jobs.intro: {name}. A pilgrim, to pray at the tomb of Peter.
work: I walked from Gaul. Four months. We buried two of our company on the way.
I came to pray for my son. He's dead. I came anyway.
worry: The roads aren't safe. Goths, bandits, hunger. We came anyway.

jobs.title: foreigner
jobs.intro: {name}. Not from here, as you can hear.
work: A foreigner has no vote, no protection of Roman law. A citizen can beat me in the street and I'd need a patron to complain.
Every few years the Senate expels someone: astrologers, philosophers, Jews, Egyptians' priests. You keep a bag packed.
worry: Some Romans think anyone who isn't Roman is a slave who hasn't been caught yet.

rise.intro: {name}. A Greek, here on business. I'm still learning these people.
work: They are the most religious people I have met, and the hardest. They'd die rather than break an oath.
They count their sons as wealth and their dead as glory. It frightens me and I admire it.
worry: One day they'll rule all the Greeks too. They don't know it yet. I do.

hero.intro: {name}. A Greek, from Neapolis, here to trade.
work: They're rustic, these Romans. No theatre to speak of, no philosophy, statues like tree stumps. And they're about to beat Pyrrhus. I don't understand it.
One of their senators told me: we don't need to be clever, we need to be right. I laughed. I'm not laughing now.
worry: They keep oaths. Not like us. It's almost a weakness. Almost.

jobs.title: citizen of the plebs
jobs.intro: {name}. Citizen. No land, no money. The census counts me only by my children.
work: I take the grain dole each month. Without it my family would starve. With it we only go hungry.
I work where there's work: the docks, the building sites. Slaves do most of it cheaper.
worry: Rent is half of everything. A room on the fifth floor, no water, no fire, and the landlord can throw us out at the Kalends.

rise.intro: {name}. Citizen. No land yet, but a citizen, and I've served.
work: I rowed in the fleet. The proletarii serve at sea when the legions have taken everyone with land. Rome wasted nobody.
The Senate's settling veterans on land in Samnium and Apulia. My name's on the list.
worry: I'm poor, and I'm Roman, and I'd do it again.

hero.intro: {name}. Citizen. No land yet. The colonies will give me some, in the Samnite country.
work: Rome sends out colonies to every hill it wins: Latin towns, Roman towns. Soon there'll be Romans from the Po to the straits.
Poor? I'm a Roman. There's no such thing as a poor Roman, only one who hasn't been given his farm yet.
worry: The Samnites are our friends now, more or less. The Umbrians too. It took fifty years of beating each other.

pleb: A room on the fourth floor on the {home}. Six of us in it. You hear everything through the walls, the births and the deaths.
My {partner} works as hard as I do. We have {kids}. We had more.
Work, eat, sleep. The baths when there's a copper to spare. Debt, always. You get used to it or you go under.
The landlord's man came again yesterday. We paid. This month.
slave: I don't have a life, stranger. I have a master. I have friends in the household, and the Saturnalia once a year.
I was born in the house. My mother was sold when I was seven. I don't know where she went.
A slave can't marry, in law. I have a woman in the household. The master allows it. He could stop allowing it.
freed: I was a slave. Now I'm a freedman. I still owe my old master days of work each year, and my respect every day.
My son will be born free. He'll never know what I know. That's what I paid for.
I have a shop, a {partner}, {kids}. People still look at the cap of freedom and see the collar.
rich: The house on the {home}, a villa at Tusculum, three hundred slaves. And debts that would ruin a smaller family.
Life is duty, the elders say: to the family, the gods, the Republic. And to whoever's in power this year, if you want to keep your head.
foreign: I send money home when I can. They think Rome is paved with gold. It's paved with other people's work.
I live across the river with the others from home. We have our own gods, our own food, and our own dead to bury.
state: I serve. Paid, fed, a pension if I live. Not many can say that.
My {partner} lives near the station. I see the {kids} when I'm off duty. Less than I'd like.
church: My life is given to God. It's easier than giving it to the world.
I was baptised at Easter. Everything before that is another life. Some of it I'd rather forget.

republic: Clodius was killed on the Appian Way by Milo's men. His people burned the Senate House as his pyre. Now Pompey's sole consul, with soldiers in the Forum.
Caesar's taken all of Gaul. A million dead, they say, and a million sold. The slave markets are full, prices down.
Crassus went east to fight the Parthians and never came back. They sent back his head.
The grain price is up again. The tribunes promise a law. There'll be a riot before there's a law.
They're buying votes openly in the tribes. A man was caught with the cash in the Campus. Nothing will happen to him.
Another block collapsed in the Subura in the night. Nobody knows how many were inside.
empire: The Emperor's old and cautious and never leaves Italy. The provinces pay, the frontiers hold, the city's fed. Nobody asks what it costs.
An informer denounced a senator for treason. His property goes to the treasury and a quarter to the informer. That's how you get rich now.
A slave killed his master on the Esquiline. By law every slave in the house dies with him. They'll do it at the Esquiline gate.
The Greens and the Blues fought after the races. Two dead by the Circus.
Christians were denounced in the Transtiberim. The magistrate let them go if they'd sacrifice. Some wouldn't.
A fever's going round the low quarters by the river. The undertakers are busy.
late: The Emperor's building a new Rome in the east. The old one gets the leftovers.
The bishop's a great man now. Men who used to buy magistracies are buying church offices.
There's been a bread riot at the Prefect's house. The soldiers cleared the street.
They say the Goths are on the Danube again. They're always on the Danube again.
The old families still sacrifice in private. The Emperor's law forbids it. The Prefect's cousins do it.
fall: Narses beat Totila in the north. The Goth king's dead. After twenty years of war, maybe it stops. Maybe.
The Pope's been kept in Constantinople for years. The Emperor wants his signature on something.
In the siege people ate grass and dogs and worse. Some didn't wake. Some weren't allowed to.
The aqueducts are cut. The baths are dry. We drink from the river and the fevers come with it.
Totila emptied the city once. Forty days with no one in it. I was hiding in the Colosseum with my mother.
early: Scipio's triumph! Carthage's gold carried through the streets, and the captives, and the elephants' tusks. He'll be called Africanus.
The treaty's signed. Carthage gives up her fleet, burns it in the harbour, and pays ten thousand talents over fifty years.
The Senate's voting land for Scipio's veterans in Samnium and Apulia.
Philip of Macedon helped Hannibal. The Senate won't forget. There'll be war in the east before long.
The poet Ennius, Cato brought him from Sardinia, is writing the whole history of Rome in verse. They say it's magnificent.
Sixteen years since Cannae. The Senate never once asked for peace. Now look at us.
heroic: Pyrrhus of Epirus has landed at Tarentum with a phalanx and twenty elephants. The consul Laevinus has marched south to meet him.
The Tarentines laughed at our envoy and fouled his toga. He said it'd be washed in their blood. Now they've hired a king. We'll see.
Blind old Appius Claudius had himself carried into the Senate: no peace while a foreign king stands in Italy. They cheered him to the roof.
Curius Dentatus finished the Samnites and the Sabines, and went home to his turnips. They're citizens now, the Sabines. Kin.
Fabricius refused Pyrrhus's gold. The king said it would be easier to turn the sun from its course than Fabricius from honour.
collapse: The Vandals were here fourteen days. They took everything: the gilded tiles off Jupiter's roof, the Temple treasure from Jerusalem, the Empress herself. Pope Leo talked them out of burning it. That's what we're grateful for now.
The Emperor Petronius Maximus ran when the Vandals came. The crowd stoned him in the street and threw him in the Tiber. He'd reigned eleven weeks.
Valentinian killed Aetius with his own hand, the one general we had. Then Aetius's men killed Valentinian on the Campus. And the crowd went to the races.
Africa's gone to the Vandals, and the grain with it. The Senate's still arguing about the seating at the games.
There'll be another emperor by winter. The barbarian generals choose them now. Bets are open on how long he lasts.

republic: Jupiter keeps the city, Vesta keeps the fire, the household gods keep the house. You keep them fed, or you pay for it.
I buried a lead tablet at the fountain against the man who cheated me. Named him, cursed his hands. It's not illegal if nobody finds it.
empire: Jupiter, Mars, the Emperor's genius, Isis for my wife, Mithras for my brother in the army. You never know which one's listening.
The dead emperors become gods. The Senate votes on it. A committee decides who's divine now.
late: My grandmother sacrificed to Jupiter. My mother lit candles to the martyrs. I do both, and hope neither finds out.
The Christians have the Emperor now. They used to be burned. Now they're in the Senate. Give it time and they'll burn someone.
fall: God is great and Rome is small. We pray at the tombs of the martyrs and hope they're listening.
The old temples are shut or they're churches now. The saints moved in when the gods moved out. Or when the gods were thrown out.
early: Jupiter Best and Greatest keeps the city. Vesta's fire keeps it alive. We keep the rites exactly, and the gods keep us.
After Cannae we did everything the Sibylline books said. We brought the Great Mother from Phrygia. And the gods turned back to Rome.
heroic: Jupiter on the Capitol, Mars on the Campus, Janus at the gate, Vesta at the hearth, and the Lares in every house. We give them what's theirs, and they give us Rome.
Decius gave himself to the gods below for the legions, and the gods took him and gave us the day. That's how it works, between Romans and gods: faith for faith.
collapse: We're all Christians now, officially. The relic sellers do a better trade than the bakers. A finger of Saint Laurence, very cheap.
Some say the old gods abandoned Rome for the Christian one. Some say the Christian one abandoned Rome for Constantinople. Either way, nobody's minding it.

bump: Hands where I can see them!
Try that again and you'll lose the hand.
night: Late to be out. The knives come out after dark.
Mind the windows: they empty the pots on your head.
puzzled: Ask the Greeks. They know about that sort of thing.

moods: Up since before dawn. I'll be up after dark.
You want to talk? I've a minute. Just a minute.
There's a lot on my mind. Money, mostly.
A bit of wine at lunch. More than a bit.
We buried my brother last week. The fever.

early: Zama! You've heard? Of course you have.
There's work to do. There always is.
I've just come from the temple. Thanks for my son's return.
My brother didn't come back. He died well.
empire: Nothing to do till the games.
A bit of wine at lunch. More than a bit.
late: Have you bread? No? Then what do you want?
fall: My children. The fever. All three.
heroic: Sentinum! My father was there. Did you know?
The harvest won't bring itself in.
You're not from here. Where's home?
It's a feast day tomorrow, or the day after, or both.
collapse: Have you heard? Another one's dead, the emperor, I mean.
Drink with me. Why not? Why not.
What do you want? Everyone wants something.
It's all ending. Might as well enjoy the races.

pleb: A small house on the {home}, my {partner}, {kids}. My sons will serve when Rome calls. That's a Roman's life, and it's enough.
We lost my father in the war and my uncle at Cannae. Their names are said at our hearth every day.
slave: I serve a hard house but an honest one. The master eats what we eat and works beside us when there's need.
Freedom comes to those who serve well. I've seen it given, and kept.
freed: I was a slave in this house. Now I'm free, and a client of my old master, and my son is a citizen. Rome keeps its word.
I stood in the line of freedmen at the census. Proudest day of my life.
rich: We have land in the Sabine country and this house on the {home}. Not large. Our ancestors lived plainly and conquered Italy.
Duty first: to the gods, to the Republic, to the family. My father said it every morning. I say it to my sons.
foreign: I came to trade and I stay because they keep their word. It's rare, believe me.
The Romans are hard to know and easy to trust.
state: I serve the magistrate as my father did. The office passes; the Republic stays.
My {partner} and {kids} live near the Capitol. I see the temple from my door every morning.
church: Our gods have kept Rome through the worst of it.

pleb: A little house on the {home}, a plot outside the gate, my {partner}, {kids}. When Rome calls, I go; when I come back, I plough.
We eat porridge and beans and sleep well. There's nothing to envy in Tarentum.
slave: I serve a small house. We work the same fields and eat the same bread.
I was taken in the Samnite wars. My master's a fair man. Most Samnites are Romans by now anyway.
freed: I was a slave, now I'm free, and a client of my old master's house. We keep faith with each other.
My son will be a citizen and serve in the legions like any Roman.
rich: We have a farm in the Sabine hills and this house on the {home}. My grandfather ploughed it himself. So do I.
Duty to the gods, to the Republic, to the family. And to the farm, or there's nothing to eat.
foreign: I'm a stranger here, and they're kind to strangers who keep their word.
They're simple, these people. Simple the way an oak is simple.
state: I serve the magistrate for his year. Next year, a different one, the same Republic.
